```{r setup, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(yardstick)
library(rpart)
library(randomForest)
library(discrim)

library(tidymodels)
library(GGally)
library(skimr)

# Read in the data
property.train <- read_csv("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/161324/assessment/data/property_train_val.csv")
property.test <- read_csv("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/161324/assessment/data/property_test.csv")
wheat.train <- read_csv("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/161324/assessment/data/wheat_train_val.csv") |>
  mutate(variety = factor(variety))
wheat.test <- read_csv("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/161324/assessment/data/wheat_test.csv")
```


## Exercise 1: Property Value Prediction

```{r}
names(property.train)
names(property.test)
#view(property.train)


##### ----- Linear Regression (Lecture Week 4)
# Linear Regression using all var
price_per_unit.lm <- lm(price_per_unit ~ ., data = property.train)
#pred <- predict(price_per_unit.lm, newdata=property.test)
#predict(price_per_unit.lm, newdata=property.test)
summary(price_per_unit.lm) # small p-value indicates statistically significant evidence.

#Linear Regression using stepwise for var
price_per_unit.lm.step <- stats::step(price_per_unit.lm) # namespace conflict stats:: no using namspace like c++??
#pred.step <- predict(price_per_unit.lm.step, newdata = property.test)
summary(price_per_unit.lm.step) # small p-value indicates statistically significant evidence.


##### Checking price per unit ranges against true values from training data 
#lm
augment(price_per_unit.lm,
        newdata=property.train,
        interval="prediction") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_linerange(
    mapping=aes(x=.fitted, ymin=.lower, ymax=.upper)) +
  geom_point(mapping=aes(x=.fitted, y=price_per_unit),
    col='red') +
  labs(x="Predicted price per unit", y="True price per unit", title = "LM")

# lm.stepwise
augment(price_per_unit.lm.step,
        newdata=property.train,
        interval="prediction") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_linerange(
    mapping=aes(x=.fitted, ymin=.lower, ymax=.upper)) +
  geom_point(mapping=aes(x=.fitted, y=price_per_unit),
    col='red') +
  labs(x="Predicted price per unit", y="True price per unit", title="Lm_stepwise")



##### ----- Decision Tree (Lecture Week 5)
price_per_unit.rp01 <- rpart(formula = price_per_unit ~ . , data = property.train, cp=0.01)
price_per_unit.rp001<- rpart(formula = price_per_unit ~ ., data = property.train, cp = 0.001)

printcp(price_per_unit.rp001) #same as lecture 5 no evidence to prefer trees past 1 split, xerror =1

#visualise tree
plot(price_per_unit.rp01,
     compress = TRUE, 
     margin = 0.1)
text(price_per_unit.rp01) # Looks unstable aswell! -- should use Random Forest

# R_Forest
set.seed(5)
property.train.bs <- slice_sample(
                   property.train,
                   n=400,
                   replace=TRUE)

bind_rows(lst(property.train,
              property.train.bs),
          .id="data") |>
  select(data, price_per_unit,
           property_age, transit_distance, nearby_stores) |> #skipping lat, long and sale time is only 2 years so skipping
  pivot_longer(-c(data, price_per_unit)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x=value, y=price_per_unit),
             alpha=0.5) +
  facet_grid(rows=vars(data),
             cols=vars(name),
             scales='free_x') +
  labs(x=NULL) #The distributions of the two datasets are similar.

price_per_unit.rf <- randomForest(price_per_unit ~ ., data = property.train, mtry = 2)

##### ----- Compare RSME
#property.train |>
#  mutate(.pred = predict(property.rp, newdata = property.train)) |>
#  summarise(MSE = mean((price_per_unit - .pred)^2))
#MSE of prediction for regression tree is 51.535. 

### if MSE with linear model is lower: suggests that the relationship between target and predictors is reasonably linear

# Compare R Squared of models
#lm <- glance(price_per_unit.lm) |> pull(r.squared)
#lm_step <- glance(price_per_unit.lm.step) |> pull(r.squared)

comp_rmse <- bind_rows(
  list(
    lm      = property.train |> mutate(.pred = predict(price_per_unit.lm,      newdata = property.train)) |> summarise(MSE = sqrt(mean((price_per_unit - .pred)^2))),
    lm_step = property.train |> mutate(.pred = predict(price_per_unit.lm.step, newdata = property.train)) |> summarise(MSE = sqrt(mean((price_per_unit - .pred)^2))),
    rpart   = property.train |> mutate(.pred = predict(price_per_unit.rp01,            newdata = property.train)) |> summarise(MSE = sqrt(mean((price_per_unit - .pred)^2))),
    rf   = property.train |> mutate(.pred = predict(price_per_unit.rf,            newdata = property.train)) |> summarise(MSE = sqrt(mean((price_per_unit - .pred)^2)))
  ),.id = "Model")
comp_rmse

#rpart performs better than linear model, regression tree performs better than both (lowest RSME).




# predict price_per_unit for every row in property_test.csv.
#property.test |>
#  bind_cols(.pred=pred) |>
#  select(.pred, everything())

#augment(price_per_unit.lm,
#        newdata=property.test,
#        interval="prediction") |>
#  select( .fitted,
#         .lower, .upper,
#         everything())

pred.rf <- predict(price_per_unit.rf, newdata = property.test)

final.pred.ex1 <- property.test |>
  bind_cols(.pred = pred.rf) |>
  select(.pred, everything())
final.pred.ex1


write_csv(final.pred.ex1, "predictions/property_price_predictions.csv")



```

### 1.1 Property Value Methodology
Exploratory analysis:
Jumped straight into Linear regression, wouldn't have had to brute force so many different models if I analysed the data before rushing in. 

Data processing:
Minimal data processing, no unusual observations or missingness found in the property dataset

Model Techniques:
Linear regression, Decision Trees, and Random Forest Tree

Tuning: 
(stepwise)[linear regression] remove variables until AIC doesn't go lower, 
(complexity parameter)[decision tree] min number of observations before a split, 
(mtry)[forest] number of input variables chosen at each split 

Final Model selected was the random forest, because of it's low RMSE score compared to linear regression and decision trees.


## Exercise 2: Wheat Variety Classification

```{r}

##### quickly looking at the data
wheat.train |> skim()
#names(wheat.test)
#view(wheat.train.flt)

#filter outliers
wheat.train.flt <- wheat.train |> filter(kernel_area < 90)

#ggpairs(glass.train, mapping = aes(col=Type), alpha=0.3) tutorial code
ggpairs(wheat.train.flt, aes(col = variety, alpha = 0.3))
# lots show linearly separable, no curving (width v. perimeter for example) -- got excited to rush into LDA
wheat.train.flt |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x=kernel_width, y=kernel_perimeter, col=variety))


##### rushed into using LDA, quickly filtered out 3 outliers and visualise to check

#visualise
wheat.train.flt |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(kernel_area, kernel_perimeter, kernel_compactness,
             kernel_length, kernel_width, kernel_asymmetry, groove_length),
    names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, y = variety, col = variety)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.1, alpha = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free_x")


##### Generative classifiers LDA, KDA, Naive Bayes. (Lecture Week 7) (linear discriminant analysis)
spec_lda <- discrim_linear()
fit_lda1 <- spec_lda |>
  fit(variety ~ ., data=wheat.train.flt)
fit_lda1 # initial model uses all variables, haven't dialed in bias-variance trade off using step() and AIC scores

#checkl
lda.pred <- fit_lda1 |> augment(new_data=wheat.train.flt)
lda.pred |> conf_mat(truth=variety, estimate=.pred_class)
# a couple Canadians being predicted as kama but otherwise accurate
lda.pred |> accuracy(truth=variety, estimate=.pred_class)
# accuracy score is 0.96, seems high.


##### Checking the assumptions of LDA (Should've done before)
# Multicollinearity check 
wheat.train.flt |>
  select(-variety) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)
# severe, especially size features (length, width etc). I either have to drop a multitude of features or use a more appropriate model

#Multivariate normality
wheat.train.flt |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -variety, names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = value)) +
  stat_qq() + stat_qq_line() +
  facet_grid(variety ~ feature, scales = "free")
#holds pretty normal, maybe slight deviation in kernal_asymmetry but nothing severe 

# homogeneity of covariances
wheat.train.flt |>
  group_by(variety) |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), var)) |>
  pivot_longer(-variety, names_to = "feature", values_to = "variance") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variety, y = variance, fill = variety)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free_y")
# Lack of homogeneity of covariances. -> kerenel_area, kernel_length, kernel_perimeter, groove_length, kernel_asymmetry. Only feature similar across all 3 varieties is kernel_width



# can't use:
# - Naive Bayes (independence assumption)
# - multinomial logistic regression (Multicollinearity)
# - Linear Discriminant Analysis 

# next best fit going forward is probably classification trees / random forest (no class volume imbalance -- no smote) else KDA/KNN (few assumptions) I'm leaving as last resort.

# decision tree //lecture boilerplate
wheat.rp <- decision_tree(
  mode = 'classification',
  min_n = 7 # usually 20 -- performs better with 7 on the ROC curve
) |>
  fit(variety ~ ., data = wheat.train.flt)

wheat.rp.pred <- wheat.rp |>
  augment(wheat.train.flt)

wheat.rp.pred |>
  conf_mat(truth = variety, estimate = .pred_class)



# or cost complexity decision tree //lecture boilerplate
wheat.rp2 <- decision_tree(
  mode = 'classification',
  cost_complexity = 0.011 #xerror value
) |>
  fit(variety ~ ., data = wheat.train.flt)

wheat.rp2.pred <- wheat.rp2 |>
  augment(wheat.train.flt)

wheat.rp2.pred |>
  conf_mat(truth = variety, estimate = .pred_class)



# forest //lecture boilerplate
set.seed(1234)
wheat.rf <- rand_forest(mode = 'classification', mtry = 2) |>
  fit(variety ~ ., data = wheat.train.flt)

wheat.rf.pred <- wheat.rf |>
  augment(wheat.train.flt)

wheat.rf.pred |>
  conf_mat(truth = variety, estimate = .pred_class)


all_preds <- bind_rows(
  list(
    lda    = lda.pred,
    tree_s7   = wheat.rp.pred,
    tree_cc   = wheat.rp2.pred,
    forest = wheat.rf.pred
  ),
  .id = "Model"
)

## ROC () -- finding best possible thresholds (sensitivity vs specificity) [closest to top left]
all_preds |>
  group_by(Model) |>
  roc_curve(
    truth = variety,
    # tidymodels auto-detects .pred_<class> columns for multiclass
    c(.pred_Canadian, .pred_Kama, .pred_Rosa)
  ) |>
  autoplot() +
  theme(legend.position = 'top')


# class imbalance (SMOTE) KNN sampling -- fairly balanced don't need
#library(themis)
#set.seed(1234)
#rec <- recipe(Status ~ ., data=covid.train) |>
#  step_smotenc(Status,
#               over_ratio = 1,
#               skip=TRUE) |>
#  prep(covid.train)
#covid.balanced <- rec |> bake(new_data=NULL)
#covid.balanced |> count(Status)



bind_rows(
  list(
    lda    = lda.pred |> accuracy(truth = variety, estimate = .pred_class),
    tree_s7   = wheat.rp.pred |> accuracy(truth = variety, estimate = .pred_class),
    tree_cc  = wheat.rp2.pred |> accuracy(truth = variety, estimate = .pred_class),
    forest = wheat.rf.pred |> accuracy(truth = variety, estimate = .pred_class) # first choice, good ROC curve, estimate closest to 1
  ),
  .id = "Model"
) |>
  select(Model, .estimate)

final.pred.ex2 <- wheat.rf |>
  augment(wheat.test)
  
final.pred.ex2 |> select(.pred_class, everything())
final.pred.ex2

write_csv(final.pred.ex2, "predictions/wheat_variety_predictions.csv")

library(rpart.plot)
rpart.plot(wheat.rp$fit)

```

### 2.1 Wheat Variety Methodology

Exploratory analysis:
Instead of rushing in this time I used a ggpairs plot and a point plot. I've left the example kernel_width against kernel_perimeter since it clearly illustrates the linearly separable, lack of curving of the data making it perfect for LDA.


Data processing:
Using the 3rd plot I found 3 outliers, one in each variety of wheat. Since these observations were unusual I decided to remove them else they would weaken the strength of my prediction model. 

Model Techniques:
LDA -> assumptions don't really hold
Classification trees
Random Forest

Tuning: 
(cost complexity / min_n)[decision tree] min number of observations before a split, 
(mtry)[forest] number of input variables chosen at each split 

Final Model selected was the random forest, because of it's good ROC curve, estimate closest to 1

### 2.2 Wheat Variety Explainability
The main Differentiators for wheat variety are, inorder; groove length < 5.6 , kernal area < 13, and >= 4.9 as shown by the decision tree.
